name: Domaine du Pégau Châteauneuf-du-Pape Cuvée Réservée 2017
text:
## Domaine du Pégau Châteauneuf-du-Pape Cuvée Réservée 2017

**The story.** Domaine du Pégau is an old name in [Châteauneuf-du-Pape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC). The Féraud family traces its roots in the village to the middle of the 17th century, when their ancestors first planted vines among their [olive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olive) and fruit trees. For generations the wine was sold to merchants (négociants), until Paul Féraud began bottling his own wine from a 5-hectare parcel he had inherited. In 1987 his daughter Laurence joined him, and from the 2005 vintage she has run the estate ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/pegau-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).

The wine used to be sold as Domaine Féraud. The new name, Pégau, is an old [Provençal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proven%C3%A7al_dialect) word for an ancient wine jug, one of which was found during excavations at the 14th-century [Palace of the Popes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais_des_Papes) in [Avignon](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Palais+des+Papes,+Avignon,+France&t=k). As for saying it, Laurence pronounces it "Pay-Go", while her father says "Puh-Gow", a debate that, as Jeff Leve says, makes for fun dinner conversation ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/pegau-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).

**The vineyards.** Pégau owns 21 hectares in Châteauneuf in 11 parcels, 19.5 of them for red grapes. The best vines are on the plateau of [La Crau](https://www.google.com/maps?q=La+Crau,+Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape,+France&t=k), on rocks, stones, clay and [limestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limestone), and the oldest were planted in 1902. In 2012 the family added 60 hectares in the [Côtes du Rhône](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%B4tes_du_Rh%C3%B4ne_AOC) near [Sorgues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sorgues), now sold as Château Pégau ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/pegau-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).

**The wine: Cuvée Réservée.** This is Pégau's main Châteauneuf, about 6,500 cases a year, and very traditionally made. It is roughly 85% [Grenache](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenache), 9% [Syrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syrah), and 4% [Mourvèdre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mourv%C3%A8dre), [Counoise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counoise) and other varieties. The grapes are not destemmed, only wild yeasts are used, the whole bunches ferment in old cement vats, and the wine ages for about two years in a collection of old foudres from 27 to 60 hectolitres, from Eastern Europe to France. The oldest is about 90 years old and made of wood from Russia ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/pegau-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)). Jeff Leve prefers it even to the longer-aged Cuvée Laurence.

For 2017, Joe Czerwinski reports about 80% Grenache with Syrah, Mourvèdre and others, and Leve "close to 80% Grenache" ([JJ Buckley, critics' notes](https://www.jjbuckley.com/wine/2017-domaine-du-pegau-chateauneuf-du-pape-cuvee-reservee/2017-381-750/)).

**The vintage.** [Jancis Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jancis_Robinson)'s [vintage chart](https://www.jancisrobinson.com/learn/vintages/southern-rhone) sums up 2017 in the southern Rhône as frost, then rain, then heat waves: not an easy year. The harvest was early and small, and the berries tiny, giving concentrated, age-worthy reds. Neighbours such as Clos des Papes and Pierre Usseglio reported heavy [coulure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coulure) on their Grenache (flowers failing to set into grapes). Pégau made a dense, backward 2017: Leve found it "one of the most concentrated sensations of the vintage".

**What the critics say for 2017.** As listed by [JJ Buckley](https://www.jjbuckley.com/wine/2017-domaine-du-pegau-chateauneuf-du-pape-cuvee-reservee/2017-381-750/):
- **[Jeb Dunnuck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeb_Dunnuck): 95** (October 2020). "Showed brilliantly", with the Provençal character of the vintage and classic Pégau notes of red and black currants, smoked herbs, cured meats, new leather and ground pepper. More like the 1999 or 2005 than the 2007 or 2009: concentrated, structured, backward, it "will evolve for 30 years or more".
- **Jeff Leve, [The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/pegau-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/): 95** (September 2019). Deep in colour; dark, spicy, ripe, sweet, fleshy and peppery, expanding on the palate. Long, fresh and juicy, it "is going to require time".
- **[Wine Advocate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wine_Advocate): 95** (Joe Czerwinski, September 2020). Pégau's distinctive violet and [garrigue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garrigue) aromas, plummy fruit and velvety tannins, with mocha and licorice on the finish. "Not as sexy out of the gate as some vintages": cellar a year or two, then drink over the next decade.
- **[Wine Spectator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wine_Spectator): 95** (James Molesworth, October 2020). Dark and winey, with steeped fig, [blackcurrant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackcurrant) and blackberry, then warm paving stone, bay leaf and tar. "A bit of patience is needed." Best 2023 to 2037.
- **[CellarTracker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CellarTracker) community: 92.2** (from your CellarTracker list).

**How it's drinking now.** In October 2026 the wine is nine years old. Your CellarTracker list gives a window of 2024 to 2032, Wine Spectator's runs to 2037, and Dunnuck gives it 30 years. Leve says Pégau is usually best with 5 to 7 years in bottle, and the best vintages drink well 7 to 25 years after the harvest ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/pegau-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)). So it is just entering its window. Old-school Pégau can be wild and earthy, with notes of leather, game and garrigue. Decant it 2 to 3 hours ahead, or keep it a few more years.

**Serving.** The Wine Cellar Insider suggests about 15.5°C, almost cellar temperature, for freshness and lift. Young vintages benefit from 1 to 3 hours in a [decanter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decantation) to soften and open the perfume; older ones need only enough to leave the sediment behind ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/pegau-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).

**Food.** The Wine Cellar Insider suggests classic meat dishes (veal, pork, beef, lamb, duck, game, roast chicken, braises, sausages, barbecue and [cassoulet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassoulet)), plus, more unusually, Asian dishes and hearty fish like [tuna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuna). My picks for this earthy, peppery style: a Provençal [daube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daube) of beef, roast [leg of lamb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamb_and_mutton) with garlic and rosemary, duck with olives, or seared tuna with a pepper crust.

**Value and where to buy.** A newer vintage is easy to find: BSW Liquor carries the 2023 Cuvée Réservée at $135 and ZYN at $106. BSW also has Château Pégau's white Côtes du Rhône Cuvée Lone at $29.99, and ZYN the Plan Pégau red at $28.20. Back vintages like the 2017 turn up with merchants such as [JJ Buckley](https://www.jjbuckley.com/wine/2017-domaine-du-pegau-chateauneuf-du-pape-cuvee-reservee/2017-381-750/) and at auction.

**From the history books**
- **The popes and their castle.** In 1309 [Pope Clement V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Clement_V) moved the papacy to [Avignon](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Palais+des+Papes,+Avignon,+France&t=k), beginning the [Avignon Papacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avignon_Papacy). His successor [John XXII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_John_XXII) improved the vineyards to the north and built the summer [castle](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Ch%C3%A2teau+des+Papes,+Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape,+France&t=k) that gave the village its name ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)). The jug that gave Pégau its name was found at the popes' palace.
- **France's first appellation.** Fraud was so common in the early 20th century that local growers, led by Baron [Pierre Le Roy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Le_Roy_de_Boiseaumari%C3%A9) of [Château Fortia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_Fortia), drew up France's first [appellation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appellation_d'origine_contr%C3%B4l%C3%A9e) rules in 1923, made law in 1936 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **From bulk to bottle.** Before World War I, much Châteauneuf was sold in bulk to [Burgundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgundy_wine) to beef up thinner wines ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)). Pégau, too, sold its wine to merchants until Paul Féraud started bottling under the family name.

**Curious details**
- **Which bottling do you have?** Pégau used to bottle the same vintage at different times, sometimes to order. Vintages from 1990 and earlier could have three bottling dates almost a year apart, and even the 2003 was bottled over six months, so bottles of the same vintage can differ. Bottling dates are standardized today ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/pegau-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).
- **Da Capo.** Pégau's legendary old-vine cuvée, Da Capo, is made only in the greatest years: so far just 1998, 2000, 2003, 2007 and 2010, about 500 cases each.
- **A clock on the bottle.** In 2013 the Plan Pégau label gained a clock on the neck, its hands pointing to the different years the blend comes from.
- **A wine with its own theme tune.** Scan the barcode on the back label of the white Cuvée A Tempo with your phone and you will hear music written for the wine.
- **The flying-cigar law.** In 1954, after local reports of [UFOs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_saucer), the Châteauneuf council banned "flying cigars" from flying over or landing in the commune. The decree is still in force ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **Strong by law.** Châteauneuf must reach at least 12.5% alcohol with no added sugar, and yields are limited to 35 hectolitres per hectare ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
